name: Piracetam

lead: Piracetam is the first of the racetams, developed at UCB in the 1960s. It is taken by mouth and prescribed in parts of Europe for cognitive decline, vertigo and myoclonus.
People in self-improvement communities take it for focus and memory, which supports their study, training and routine consistency rather than changing appearance directly.

paras: Its mechanism is not settled. Proposed actions include mild AMPA receptor modulation, effects on acetylcholine and NMDA signalling, and improved blood cell flexibility and microcirculation.

Reported effects include anxiety, insomnia, irritability, headache and agitation. It lowers platelet aggregation, so it is contraindicated in brain haemorrhage, and kidney impairment slows clearance. It is prescription-only in the UK and not FDA-approved in the US.

chain: Used for focus, memory and mental energy
More consistent studying, training and routine
angle.text: Piracetam is used as a cognitive supplement, so its link to looks runs through routine: people stack it with training, study and sleep protocols hoping for more focus and mental stamina. It does not act on skin, hair or physique directly.

lead: Piracetam is the original racetam, a synthetic nootropic first made in the 1960s by Corneliu Giurgea at UCB in Belgium and the compound for which the word "nootropic" was coined.[1][2] People who take it do so mainly for focus, memory and mental sharpness, which feeds into how they look through the chain of better studying and work output, steadier routines and, in some stacks, recovery from head-related fatigue; it has no direct effect on skin, hair or bone structure.

It is a cyclic derivative of GABA, taken by mouth, and is excreted largely unchanged by the kidneys.[2][3] It is prescribed in the UK for cortical myoclonus and in many European and other countries for cognitive decline, vertigo and related complaints, while in the United States it is not FDA-approved and its inclusion in supplements is unlawful.[1][2]

Research includes clinical trials in dementia, mild cognitive impairment, stroke, aphasia, vertigo, dyslexia and concussion, plus reviews of nootropic use by healthy people and students.[4][5][6][3][7][8][9] Results vary by condition and by review, and trials in healthy people are limited.
infobox: Rx in UK and Australia; not FDA-approved in US; OTC in some countries[1]

paras: Piracetam has no direct cosmetic use. Looksmaxxing-adjacent users take it as a general cognitive aid to support focus on studying, work and self-improvement routines, sometimes alongside choline sources or other racetams.[4][5]

In the UK it is approved for adults with cortical myoclonus, and in a number of European countries it is sold for age-related cognitive decline, vertigo and post-stroke problems.[1][3] Japan lists it as prescription-only, while the Czech Republic and Hungary sell it over the counter.[1]

Early controlled trials examined piracetam in chronic brain failure in older adults and in post-concussional syndrome, reporting outcomes in memory, symptom scores and daily function.[10][11] A 1986 report reviewed its effects in developmental dyslexia, and a 1991 randomized trial studied it in elderly motorists.[12][13]

A 12-month registered trial enrolled 676 people with mild cognitive impairment, and a 1998 trial of 571 people tested it for aphasia after middle cerebral artery stroke; the latter was terminated.[8][9] Reviews of vertigo treatment have assessed its effectiveness, and a trial compared it with dimenhydrinate in peripheral vertigo.[14][15] A 2012 Cochrane review examined its use for fetal distress in labour.[16]

Reviews of nootropics in healthy people describe popularity among students and workers and note that effects in non-impaired brains are still being assessed.[4][5] Wikipedia summarises Cochrane and other reviews, including a 2001 review that found insufficient evidence in dementia.[1]

Reported effects include anxiety, insomnia, irritability, headache, agitation, tremor, drowsiness and weight gain.[1] Because it reduces platelet aggregation, it is contraindicated in cerebral haemorrhage, and dose reduction is advised in kidney impairment since elimination slows.[1][2] Acute toxicity in animals is very low.[1]

No single mechanism is established.[6] Proposed actions include weak positive modulation of AMPA receptors, effects on cholinergic and NMDA systems, calcium channel inhibition, improved membrane fluidity and better red blood cell deformability.[1][2][6][7]
Oral absorption is nearly complete, with peak plasma levels about an hour after a fasted dose and a plasma half-life near five hours; it is not significantly metabolised.[2]

Piracetam (2-oxo-1-pyrrolidine acetamide) is a white crystalline powder very soluble in water.[2] It was synthesised in 1964 at UCB, initially as an analogue explored for motion sickness, and marketed from 1971 as a cognitive enhancer.[1][2] It founded the racetam family, which includes aniracetam, oxiracetam and phenylpiracetam, and is structurally related to the antiepileptic levetiracetam.[6]

In the United States piracetam is sold through gray-market channels despite lacking FDA approval.[1] A 2020 study found racetam-type drugs in cognitive-enhancement supplements.[1] A systematic review of student use lists piracetam among drugs taken as study aids.[5]
